analysis.one_liner: Makes the Freedom of Information Act apply to Congress, letting citizens request members' records.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan-backed disclosure bill from 20 House Republicans died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Today the Freedom of Information Act—the law that lets citizens request government records—does not apply to Congress. This bill would change that, making members of Congress subject to the same records-disclosure rules as executive agencies. It includes one carve-out: your personal casework files and correspondence with your own representative would stay private. The bill was referred to the House Government Operations Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Citizens who want to see how their representatives conduct their official business, journalists, and watchdog groups, because they could use FOIA requests to obtain congressional records that are currently withheld. Ordinary people would keep a privacy protection too: their personal casework files and letters to their own representative would remain exempt from disclosure.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes section 552 of title 5—the Freedom of Information Act—apply to the Congress, closing the gap that lets members withhold their official records from public records requests.
It amends the definition of 'authority' in the Administrative Procedure Act so that Congress is no longer excluded from the disclosure law.
It exempts casework and constituent correspondence from disclosure, so voters' personal files with congressional offices stay private while members' other records become available.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, who would lose their current ability to keep official records out of public reach and would bear the cost of processing disclosure requests. Lobbyists and insiders who benefit from keeping congressional records secret would also lose.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their staffs

drawbacks.text: Applying an executive-branch disclosure statute to a co-equal branch of government raises separation-of-powers questions; Congress has historically governed its own records rather than submitting to a law administered by executive courts and agencies.

The casework and constituent-correspondence exemption creates a large category of member activity that stays secret, so the bill is narrower than a full transparency law—records tied to constituent service could still be withheld.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit—citizens being able to request the records of the branch that writes the laws—is substantial and the design is reasonably careful: it preserves voter privacy by exempting casework and constituent mail. The main cost falls on members of Congress and their staffs, who would have to process requests and operate under outside scrutiny. The chief honest objection is constitutional: FOIA was written for executive agencies, and applying it to Congress by statute may not be the cleanest legal vehicle for congressional transparency.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Government Operations Committee and then to a subcommittee, and neither ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 9, 1991, by Representative Boehner with nine original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Government Operations the same day, and three days later referred to its Subcommittee on Government Information, Justice and Agriculture.
The subcommittee took no further action; the bill never received a markup or a floor vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress, who kept their exemption from the Freedom of Information Act and continued to control access to their own records.

for.name: Rep. John A. Boehner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to apply FOIA to Congress and recruited original cosponsors.

for.name: 19 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill; no Democrat cosponsored.

for.name: Representatives Klug, Gilchrest, Hobson, Zimmer, Santorum, Zeliff, Doolittle, Riggs, and Nussle
for.what_they_did: Joined Boehner as the bill's nine original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Committee on Government Operations
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never reported it out, keeping it from reaching the House floor.

against.name: Subcommittee on Government Information, Justice and Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 11, 1991 and held no markup or vote on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 sponsors—Boehner and 19 cosponsors—were Republicans, and the Democratic-majority committee that controlled the bill's fate never acted on it.

industries.note: Because the bill died, members kept their exemption from the Freedom of Information Act and retained control over which of their official records become public. That interest runs against voters' interest in seeing how their representatives work, though the bill would have kept constituents' own casework files private.
